title: Last seeing Oliver in 1937 and the dozens story at rehearsal
summary: Howard saw a sick Oliver in Nashville in 1937 and tells how Oliver reacted when Barney kept asking him to turn on his stand light.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Remembering King Oliver: the man, the band, the decline

blocks.x: Street clothes. You know, remember I told you they went on the change clothes? Yeah, that's why I was asking you. Well, Joe wore tuxedos, that band wore tuxedo early. See, later on I went down to Warwick's club, Wallace Tyler's place, and worked with King Oliver. And then later on, that's when Jean Starr and Justine McKinney made all that money off of some day sweetheart. Man, it was a shame the money we made when you think about it now. Why did you do without money? My mother. A lot of my money got lost in the crash. Just like I sent money home from my trip. She'd bang it for me. All right. Yep. When was the last time you saw Joe? Oliver, 1937. I was with Earl Hines and saw him in Nashville, Tennessee. 37? Well, that's when he died.
That's the year he died. What was he doing then? He was playing.

How did you play it? Well I didn't hear the band. It was in the daytime. See, we were playing the Paramount Theater in Nashville, Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday. And we played Chattanooga, I don't know, Main Street or the State Theater, the first three days. And then Nashville? Uh-huh. Joe was in Nashville?
He had a dance to play.
How was he making out then?
Well, he seemed very ill then. He didn't seem well. He didn't. He carried on so much foolishness, he didn't know whether he was real sick or not.
What kind of foolishness? Just getting around?
You can't put this in a book.

It's just not a book. It's just between us. Barney. Sure come to rehearsal one day, you know what the dozens is, don't you? Playing the dozens? No, man. Talking about a guy's mother kidding about his mother. You know, saying bad things about him. Yeah. Well, Joe said he dreamt about his mother. He had a dream about his mother. And in his dream, his mother told him to stop playing the dozens, see. So I'm not playing the dozens anymore. So Joe had a light on his music rack. So he was dark, you know. Barney on this end. I'm sitting here, Albert Nicholas here and Barney here. Barney kept saying, Joe. Turn the light on. I can't see. Joe said, okay. He got tired of it. I'm sitting in the front. Listen you mammy fucker. That was his idea of Joe playing it. That Barney kiddin him because he knew he wasn't going to put him in the dozens, see. Yeah. But he stopped him. Got off the bandstand and walked around in front and come over there and said that to him. I'm telling you, oh, we like to die. And Barney sitting up looking like a little kid, you know. Maybe one or two. Because to me when I first saw him, because now Nick's the one. I don't know how old Albert is but he's up there too. He's older than you. Nick is quite a bit older than you. I'm going to ask his first wife.
Where is she in New York?
No, Chicago. Chicago. Did you ever meet her?
Yeah. I'm sure she'll tell me. I'll go all the time I've seen her. I never thought to ask.
